claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 has residual porosity.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 has limited mechanical strength under corrosive plating-bath conditions.
Adding approximately 1–3 wt% Ni to ZrB2 during spark plasma sintering will permit densification at about 2000 °C.
Ni acts as a low-melting transient-liquid-phase former in ZrB2 at the proposed sintering temperature.
The transient liquid phase enhances particle rearrangement during sintering.
The transient liquid phase enhances grain-boundary diffusion and mass transport during sintering.
Enhanced rearrangement and mass transport produce a denser and more uniform ZrB2 microstructure.
Ni-assisted sintering eliminates or reduces open and residual pores in ZrB2.
Reduced porosity minimizes pathways by which corrosive plating-bath species penetrate the ceramic.
Minimizing corrosive-species pathways reduces pore formation and component degradation during prolonged plating-bath exposure.
Ni-doped ZrB2 sintered near 2000 °C will be finer-grained than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Ni-doped ZrB2 sintered near 2000 °C will be denser and contain fewer holes than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Microstructural refinement is expected to improve mechanical properties.
Ni-doped ZrB2 will retain superior mechanical properties during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure compared with conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Ni-doped ZrB2 will have superior corrosion resistance during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure compared with conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 is more prone to pore development and failure during long-term liquid plating-bath exposure.
The proposed performance boundary is extended exposure under typical liquid plating-bath conditions.

contradictions.description: The stated comparison baseline is conventionally sintered ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C, but the experiment instead prepares both the doped and undoped groups by spark plasma sintering at about 2000 °C. Thus, the experimental control is not the stated conventional baseline.

The falsification rule requires demonstrating a statistically significant decrease in sintering temperature, but both groups are tested at the same single target temperature. The design therefore cannot directly measure a decrease in required sintering temperature.
